```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from scripts/90_report_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Planned study
This study is designed but not yet built. The page will be updated as the analysis runs.
It is a companion to the [fuel phenology regions page](index.html) and the
[NPN curing study](npn_study.html).
:::

## At a glance

**The question.** At the scale of a region and a season, does the green-up and curing of
grasses and other herbaceous plants shape fire activity? The regions work built typical
green-up and curing dates for every 4 km cell, and both its ground check and the NPN curing
study found that weather rules don't beat the typical date against single-plant ground
dates. Fire activity is a regional, fuel-bed-scale response, the scale fire managers care
about, and it is the one verification source with good coverage of herbaceous fuels in the
Southwest and California.

**Two tests.**

1. **Seasonal:** does each region's fire season open and close at green-up and curing, for
   example a spring window on last year's cured grass that closes at green-up, and a fall
   window that opens at curing?
2. **Year to year:** in years when curing or green-up runs early or late, does fire activity
   shift with it, once dead-fuel dryness and the number of ignitions are accounted for? The
   answer is how much the phenology improves predictions for years left out of the fit, not
   a correlation.

A third question comes from partners in the northern Plains: in mixed prairie, does fire
activity dip in the gap between the cool-season and warm-season growth pulses?

## Design

| Element | Choice |
|---|---|
| Fire starts | FPA-FOD 7th edition (1992–2024): wildfires reaching 10 acres or more, by discovery week, all causes; lightning and human separately for 2001–2019 |
| Fire growth | VIIRS active fire (S-NPP, 2012 onward): unique 375 m pixel-days |
| Burned area | MTBS, by start date (large fires) |
| Phenology | Yearly satellite green-up (NDVI 20 %) and curing (NDVI end of season, 50 %) dates for every 4 km cell, 2001–2025, and the typical-date maps |
| Dead-fuel baseline | 1000-hour dead fuel moisture computed from PRISM (NFDRS equations); checks: Keetch–Byram drought index and 30-day mean vapour pressure deficit |
| Weather | PRISM daily 4 km only |
| Herbaceous cover | NLCD grassland, shrub/scrub, pasture/hay and herbaceous wetland share; in the upper Midwest and Great Plains, phenology from cells at least 35 % herbaceous |
| Unit | Region × week × year, herbaceous cells |
| Model | One pooled count model with region effects; skill judged leaving one year out |
| Years | 2001–2024 for fire starts; 2012–2024 where starts and growth overlap |
| Pilot regions | Monsoon Southwest (3), interior West (6, 12), California annual grasslands (11), northern and central Great Plains (10), upper Midwest (13) |

: Study design {.striped}

The FPA-FOD record holds wildfires only: planned ignitions (prescribed fires) were left out
when the database was built, except prescribed fires that escaped and needed suppression
(Short 2014). Fire names that look like prescribed burns are counted by region as a check.
Agricultural and prescribed burning are screened out (fire records coded as debris or open
burning; satellite detections on cropland or not linked to a reported fire), and the share
each screen removes is reported by region. In the northern Plains and upper Midwest a
snow-off date from PRISM is part of the baseline, because spring fire there depends on
snowmelt as well as green-up.

## First look: fire records (October 17)

The FPA-FOD 7th edition holds 2.66 million records for 1992–2024. For 2001–2024 in the lower 48,
1.94 million fall on the analysis grid; 193,000 reached 10 acres or more and were not debris or
open burning, 52,900 of them in the six pilot regions. Fire names that look like prescribed
burns are negligible (under 20 per region).

| Region | Fires ≥ 10 ac | Lightning | Human | Unknown cause | Debris share of human fires ≥ 10 ac | On strict herbaceous cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 Monsoon Southwest | 9,051 | 51 % | 43 % | 6 % | 13 % | 68 % |
| 6 Interior West | 9,603 | 57 % | 40 % | 3 % | 15 % | 71 % |
| 12 Interior West | 5,161 | 41 % | 54 % | 5 % | 15 % | 75 % |
| 11 California annual grasslands | 9,349 | 4 % | 68 % | 27 % | 6 % | 64 % |
| 10 Northern and central Great Plains | 12,355 | 40 % | 53 % | 7 % | 18 % | 70 % |
| 13 Upper Midwest | 7,405 | 4 % | 85 % | 12 % | 36 % | 5 % |

: Wildfires of 10 acres or more (debris and open burning removed), 2001–2024 {.striped}

**Seasonal shape.** The share of each region's fires by month already shows the windows the
study is about:

| Region | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 2 | 5 | 7 | 10 | 13 | 23 | 20 | 11 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 6 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 13 | 36 | 31 | 10 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| 12 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 6 | 20 | 35 | 22 | 9 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| 11 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 11 | 22 | 24 | 17 | 11 | 7 | 2 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 2 | 6 | 6 | 3 | 8 | 29 | 26 | 11 | 5 | 3 | 1 |
| 13 | 1 | 2 | 13 | 36 | 16 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 9 | 5 | 1 |

: Percent of each region's fires of 10 acres or more by discovery month {.striped}

The upper Midwest (13) has a sharp spring peak (March–May, 65 %) that collapses in June, and a
smaller fall rise in October: the dormant-grass windows on either side of the growing season.
The Great Plains (10) shows a human-caused March–April window before green-up and a summer
lightning season. In the monsoon Southwest (3) human fires run February–June and lightning
fires peak in June–July, before the monsoon greens the grass.

**Data issues found.**

- *Reporting change from 2020.* Records switch from separate federal and non-federal sources
  to a single interagency source in 2020–2021. Yearly counts stay continuous, but the share
  with an unknown cause rises in every pilot region (to 10–30 %), and in California (11) to
  50–86 % in 2020–2024, mostly state and local records. Splitting lightning from human starts
  is reliable only to 2019 in California, and less reliable after 2019 elsewhere.
- *Fire locations in the upper Midwest.* Only 5 % of region 13's fires are on strict
  herbaceous cells; the typical fire cell is 1 % grassland and shrub, 14 % open herbaceous
  including pasture and hay, and 37 % cropland. Herbaceous fuels there sit in small patches
  (pasture, roadsides, conservation grassland, wetland edges) inside mixed cells, so a cover
  filter would drop most of the region's fires. Fire density still rises about five-fold from
  the least to the most herbaceous cells, and the seasonal shape is the same at every level of
  cover, so these are fires in herbaceous patches. Herbaceous wetland matters here: fire cells
  hold 5 % on average against 1.4 % for the region. The satellite green-up and curing dates of
  a typical cell in this region (52 % cropland) mostly describe crops.

**How the study handles them (decided October 17).** The main outcome counts fires of all
causes, which run continuously through the reporting change; lightning and human starts are
compared for 2001–2019 only (California: totals only), with a check that counts
unknown-cause fires as human, since their seasonal pattern matches human fires (r 0.90–1.00).
Lightning fire counts are no longer used as an ignition term. In the upper Midwest every fire
is kept, herbaceous wetland counts as herbaceous fuel, and the green-up and curing timing comes
from cells that are at least 35 % herbaceous (also in the Great Plains), applied to the whole
region; fires in the most herbaceous third of cells are a check.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 1 2026 | Fire activity as a regional, seasonal check on phenology, not fire by fire | Removes the scale mismatch between fires and point observations |
| Oct 17 2026 | A companion study with its own page; code shared with the regions work | Uses the regions, satellite dates and typical-date maps directly |
| Oct 17 2026 | PRISM as the only weather source; dead-fuel moisture computed from it | One weather source across the project keeps the methods simple |
| Oct 17 2026 | FPA-FOD 7th edition (1992–2024), MTBS, VIIRS S-NPP | Long record of starts; consistent single-sensor growth series |
| Oct 17 2026 | Main outcome: wildfires of 10 acres or more by week, by cause | Fuel condition decides whether a start grows; larger fires are reported consistently |
| Oct 17 2026 | Pilot regions 3, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 13 | Grass and shrub fire regimes in the West, plus the northern Plains and upper Midwest partners |
| Oct 17 2026 | Main outcome counts all causes; lightning vs human for 2001–2019 only; California totals only | Cause reporting changed in 2020–21 (unknown causes up to 50–86 % in California); total counts are unaffected |
| Oct 17 2026 | No lightning-count ignition term; a 2020-onward indicator as a check | Lightning counts were relabelled after 2019 and are partly the outcome |
| Oct 17 2026 | Upper Midwest: all fires kept; herbaceous wetland counted as fuel; phenology from cells at least 35 % herbaceous (also Great Plains) | Fires sit in small herbaceous patches inside cropland cells, whose satellite dates track crops |

: Study decisions {.striped}
